ledger.sentence: DXA, also written DEXA, stands for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a scan that measures bone density.
ledger.note: Trust page: "a special type of x-ray technology called dual energy x-ray absorptiometry"; quick and painless bone scan.

ledger.sentence: The scan is used to help diagnose osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker.
ledger.note: Basic definition; sources describe osteoporosis assessment and fracture risk. No specific page retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The NHS describes a DEXA scan as a test that uses low-dose X-rays.
ledger.note: Retrieved NHS/trust text says DEXA uses low-dose X-rays; no text retrieved saying the NHS "lists" it among X-ray tests.

ledger.sentence: NHS trust pages say a doctor can refer a person for a DEXA scan if they may be at risk of osteoporosis, and the criteria differ between services.
ledger.note: The NHS 111 Wales eligibility text was not retrieved. Trust pages say a doctor can refer someone who may be at risk; trust criteria differ (one starts at over 40, another over 50 with intermediate or high FRAX).

ledger.sentence: One NHS trust referral form lists being a current smoker and having had a previous low-trauma fracture among the risk factors it asks about.
ledger.note: Only one trust referral form was retrieved listing current smoker and previous low-trauma fracture as ticked risk factors; no NHS 111 Wales text on under-50s.

ledger.sentence: A doctor usually makes the referral.
ledger.note: Trust pages: referrals usually come from a GP or hospital consultant; people generally cannot self-refer.

ledger.sentence: Results are combined with a fracture risk assessment rather than used alone.
ledger.note: Guideline text: BMD results should not be reviewed in isolation; fracture risk tools such as FRAX combine density with other factors (NHS formulary guideline, RUH leaflet).

ledger.sentence: The person lies on their back on a flat table.
ledger.note: Lying on back on a flat X-ray table is supported; "padded" was not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: A scanning arm passes slowly over the body, usually the hip and lower spine.
ledger.note: NHS text: arm passes slowly over the area, usually hip and lower spine. Nothing retrieved about images going to a computer.

ledger.sentence: NHS pages describe the scan as quick and painless, and the time it takes varies between services.
ledger.note: Sources give different times: NHS "usually 10 to 20 minutes", trusts ~10 minutes, up to 15 minutes, ~1 minute per scan. "5 to 15" not in any retrieved text.

ledger.sentence: The dose is low.
ledger.note: NHS: DEXA uses much lower radiation than a standard X-ray, about the same as natural exposure over roughly 3 days.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray, similar to what a person is exposed to naturally over about three days.
ledger.note: Royal Marsden leaflet not retrieved; the "extremely small" wording and "no side effects" are not in retrieved text. A Royal Brompton page gave a numerical risk but is not the cited source.

ledger.sentence: The T-score compares a person's bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus (US source) and UK NHS formulary text: T-score compares density with a healthy young adult of the same sex.

ledger.sentence: Scores are grouped into bands described as normal, low bone density (osteopenia) and osteoporosis.
ledger.note: Normal/osteopenia/osteoporosis bands supported (WHO classification in NHS trust text), but "the laboratory report shows the bands used" not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: Osteoporosis is diagnosed using the lowest T-score across the lumbar spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the total hip.
ledger.note: ROS-attributed summary in an NHS formulary guideline: osteoporosis diagnosed by T-score in lumbar spine, femoral neck and sites, using the lowest value. Secondary source; total hip listed in US NOF-style guidance.

ledger.sentence: The Z-score compares a person with others of the same age, and it is used mainly for premenopausal women, men under 50 and children.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus (US source): Z-score may be used if premenopausal, male under 50, or a child; compares with people of same age, sex, weight, ethnicity.

ledger.sentence: A T-score does not decide treatment alone.
ledger.note: Guideline text: BMD alone has high specificity but low sensitivity; results should not be reviewed in isolation.

ledger.sentence: UK osteoporosis guidance uses a fracture risk tool such as FRAX, which estimates the chance of a broken bone over ten years from bone density and other risk factors, so bone density alone does not decide treatment.
ledger.note: The ROS page was not retrieved. Ten-year fracture probability appears in the NOGG-linked FRAX review, not attributed to ROS.

ledger.sentence: A DXA scan is painless: the person lies on a flat table while a scanning arm passes over the hip and lower spine.
ledger.note: Painless supported; "padded table" not retrieved; hip and lower spine supported.

ledger.sentence: The radiation dose is low: the NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray.
ledger.note: Royal Marsden leaflet not retrieved; NHS says much lower dose than a standard X-ray.

ledger.sentence: The T-score compares bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
ledger.note: MedlinePlus (US source): compares with a healthy young adult of the same sex.

ledger.sentence: Treatment decisions use an assessment of the overall chance of breaking a bone, not the scan result alone.
ledger.note: Ten-year fracture risk idea is in FRAX/NOGG sources, but not the ROS page; "rests on" overstates.

ledger.sentence: A bone density scan measures bone density and helps to judge the risk of a fracture.
ledger.note: NHS: results used alongside a fracture risk assessment and to decide on treatment; MedlinePlus: used to predict future fracture risk.

ledger.sentence: Unlike an ordinary X-ray, it can detect small reductions in bone density, so osteoporosis can be found before a bone breaks.
ledger.note: NHS: unlike ordinary X-rays, DEXA scans can measure tiny reductions in bone density, allowing diagnosis of osteoporosis before a bone breaks.

ledger.sentence: The NHS lists reasons for a scan that include breaking bones easily, long-term use of steroid medicines, and early menopause.
ledger.note: NHS lists breaking bones easily, long-term steroids, early menopause (before 45 without HRT) as risk factors; 'minor fall' wording not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says the scan uses a low dose of radiation and the risks are much lower than with standard X-rays.
ledger.note: NHS says risks are much lower than with standard X-rays and the dose is low; 'very safe' not found.

ledger.sentence: Pregnancy is the main caution: the NHS says bone density scans and X-rays are not recommended in pregnancy.
ledger.note: NHS: scans like this are not recommended in pregnancy as X-rays can harm an unborn child, though the dose is very low; trusts ask to tell staff.

ledger.sentence: The person lies on their back on a flat, open X-ray table while a scanning arm passes slowly over them.
ledger.note: Sources describe lying on one's back on a flat, open X-ray table with a scanning arm passing over; 'no tunnel' not stated.

ledger.sentence: An NHS trust page says no special preparation is needed, although metal fasteners on clothing may need to be removed.
ledger.note: Royal Devon/trust pages: no special preparation; clothing with metal fasteners such as zips or buckles usually has to come off.

ledger.sentence: A scan result does not necessarily predict whether a person will break a bone.
ledger.note: NHS 111 Wales: results of a bone density scan will not necessarily predict whether you get a fracture.
